description_full: WEX Inc. operates a commerce platform in the United States and internationally. The Mobility segment offers fleet payment solutions, transaction processing, and information management services; and provides account activation and account retention services; authorization and billing inquiries, and account maintenance services; account management; credit and collections services; merchant services; analytics solutions; and ancillary services and offerings. This segment markets its products directly and indirectly to businesses and government agencies with fleets of commercial vehicles; and indirectly through co-branded and private label relationships. The Corporate Payments segment provides payment solutions, including embedded payments; and accounts payable automation and spend management solutions. This segment also markets its products directly and indirectly to customers in travel, fintech, insurance, consumer bill pay, and media verticals. The Benefits segment offers software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform for consumer directed healthcare benefits and full-service benefit enrollment solutions. In addition, its SaaS platform includes embedded payment solutions and plan administration services for consumer-directed health benefits; COBRA accounts; and benefit enrollment and administration services. Further, it offers custodial and depository services for health savings accounts; and markets its products through third-party administrators, financial institutions, payroll providers, and health plans. WEX Inc. was formerly known as Wright Express Corporation and changed its name to WEX Inc. in October 2012. WEX Inc. was founded in 1983 and is headquartered in Portland, Maine.

financial_summary: WEX Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $6.0B market cap on $2.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 25% against a 8% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $314M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 13.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 25% operating margin runs 18pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.07x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 24% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 10% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 1.02, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.06 vs 5y 1.02), so read it loosely.
About $97.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 65% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 75% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 75% below its DCF fair value of $717, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 76%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $441 to $1,199 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 15.6 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 6.1 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 19.0 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 27% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 5.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $202 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 25% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 17pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.68).
It converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow, or 8% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.49x.
ROE of 25% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (11.7x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 3.8% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $380.3M (6% of market cap).
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.87 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.2% over 3 years, 11.3% over 5 years and 12.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 10% of profits supports about 2.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -16.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 9% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 30%.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (5.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.4%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (27 sales, net $51.8M sold).
It returns 13.4% a year to shareholders (13.4% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 5.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 10.9% of the float, 4.7 days to cover.
people: With about 6,600 employees, each generates about $403K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and revenue has grown 13.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $48K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.1M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
